description: A cooperative microbial developmental process in which bacterial communities transition into structured biofilms. In this text, it is presented as closely interconnected with quorum sensing and as involving maturation and dispersion-related transitions.

A cell-cell communication process that synchronizes gene expression in response to bacterial population density. It is described as being activated in formed biofilms and as coordinating biofilm maturation and disassembly/dispersion.

The process by which bacterial populations embedded in a self-produced extracellular matrix establish a biofilm lifestyle. It is a central process in the abstract and is linked to quorum sensing and population density thresholds.

The microbial populations that undergo biofilm formation and participate in quorum sensing-mediated coordination. They are described as living embedded in an extracellular matrix during biofilm development.
The extracellular material produced by bacterial communities that embeds cells within a biofilm. It is a structural molecular feature supporting biofilm formation and maintenance.
The regulated transcriptional output synchronized by quorum sensing in response to population density. It is the downstream biological process through which quorum sensing exerts coordination.
The density of bacterial cells in a population, used here as the contextual trigger for quorum sensing activation. It functions as a threshold-like quantitative context for signaling.
The sessile community state adopted by bacteria during biofilm growth. It is contrasted with dispersion and is suggested to be coordinated by quorum sensing.
The developmental progression of a biofilm toward a more mature structured state. The text states that quorum sensing activates this process in formed biofilms.
The breakdown or dismantling of established biofilm structure. It is described as being activated in a coordinated manner by quorum sensing.
The process by which cells disperse from a biofilm into a more motile or planktonic state. The review emphasizes this as an emergent concept activated by quorum sensing.

Pathogenic bacterial species used as examples in the review to illustrate quorum sensing and biofilm dispersion. They represent the bacterial populations in which the described processes were observed.

A bacterial population stratum used as one of the two Gram-type groups discussed in the biofilm study. It serves as a subject class for comparing biofilm formation, matrix composition, adhesion, and dispersal mechanisms, especially in mixed-community and infection contexts.

A bacterial population stratum used as one of the two Gram-type groups discussed in the biofilm study. It is central to comparisons of biofilm development, regulation, and matrix-associated features, and is highlighted as prominent in c-di-GMP-mediated regulation.

Matrix-enclosed bacterial aggregates formed by Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. In this context, biofilm formation, development, regulation, and dispersal are the main biological processes under study, with relevance to antimicrobial resistance, biofouling, and infection persistence.

A detrimental outcome caused by biofilm formation on industrial surfaces. It is identified as a root-cause consequence of biofilms and represents an applied endpoint relevant to contamination, surface colonization, and operational loss.

A clinically and biologically relevant endpoint associated with biofilms during infections. The text emphasizes biofilm-associated resistance as a major functional consequence that complicates treatment and motivates common therapeutic strategies.

The process by which bacteria adhere, aggregate, and develop matrix-enclosed communities. It is discussed as a conserved theme across Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria and as a target for therapeutic disruption.

The staged progression of biofilm maturation, including initial adhesion, matrix accumulation, and later community organization. The paper focuses on common components present at each stage of this process.
The molecular and signaling control of biofilm formation, maturation, and dispersal. The text highlights c-di-GMP and quorum sensing as regulatory themes, with differences between Gram-type bacteria.

The early attachment step in biofilm development where bacteria adhere to surfaces. It is described as involving lipopolysaccharides and cell wall glyco-polymers in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
A protein assembly process implicated in biofilm structure and maintenance. The text suggests that inhibiting this polymerization may affect biofilms of both Gram-type bacteria.
Structural constituents of the biofilm extracellular matrix. These components are targets for enzymatic degradation and are functionally important for biofilm integrity and persistence.
An enzymatic agent proposed to degrade biofilm matrix components. It is discussed as a potential disruptor of both Gram-type biofilms by breaking down matrix polysaccharides.
A nuclease enzyme used as a matrix-degrading agent in biofilm disruption. It may degrade extracellular DNA within the matrix and thereby destabilize both Gram-positive and Gram-negative biofilms.
Vesicular structures present in biofilms and noted as a common feature across Gram-type bacteria. Their functional role is highlighted as potentially important but requiring further investigation.
A bacterial second messenger involved in genetic regulation of biofilm behavior. The text identifies it as a prominent regulator in Gram-negative bacteria.

A cell-density-dependent signaling process that regulates bacterial community behavior. In this text, it is proposed as a common regulatory mechanism during biofilm dispersal across Gram-type bacteria.
The process by which bacteria exit or break down established biofilms. It is discussed as being regulated by quorum sensing and relevant to therapeutic disruption of mixed biofilms.

A general therapeutic concept referring to treatments intended to act across mixed biofilms and both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. It is motivated by conserved biofilm features and shared regulatory themes.

Biofilm communities containing both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. They represent the mixed microbial population context motivating the search for broadly effective anti-biofilm strategies.
The environmental or clinical context in which bacterial interactions and mixed biofilms occur. It frames the relevance of biofilm formation, resistance, and dispersal beyond laboratory cultures.

Surface-associated bacterial molecules implicated in initial adhesion during biofilm formation. The text notes similar roles for LPS in Gram-negative bacteria and analogous cell wall glyco-polymers in Gram-positive bacteria.

Cell wall-associated polymeric features implicated in initial adhesion in Gram-positive bacteria. They are presented as functionally analogous to lipopolysaccharides in Gram-negative bacteria during early biofilm attachment.

A Gram-negative anaerobic bacterium discussed as a key microbial factor in oral carcinogenesis. In this review, it is described as a periodontal pathogen originating from the oral cavity and as a potential contributor to cancer-promoting inflammation, proliferation, invasion, and immune evasion.

The disease outcome of interest in the review, representing malignant transformation in the oral cavity. It is the endpoint potentially associated with Fusobacterium nucleatum-mediated inflammation and biofilm-associated microbial enrichment.

The biological process of cancer initiation and development in oral tissues. The text frames this as a process potentially influenced by Fusobacterium nucleatum through inflammatory and pro-tumor mechanisms.

A host biological response highlighted as a central mechanism in malignancy initiation and progression. In the text, inflammation is linked to Fusobacterium nucleatum-mediated cancer promotion and is implicated in oral cancer development.
A cellular growth process that can be activated by Fusobacterium nucleatum according to the review. Its stimulation is presented as one mechanism by which the bacterium may promote cancer.

A process involving the ability of cells to invade surrounding tissues. The review states that Fusobacterium nucleatum can promote cellular invasion, supporting a pro-metastatic or pro-invasive cancer phenotype.

A persistent inflammatory state described as one of the mechanisms by which Fusobacterium nucleatum may contribute to cancer development. It is relevant as a long-term pro-tumor microenvironmental process.

A cancer-related biological process in which abnormal cells avoid immune detection or elimination. The review identifies immune evasion as a mechanism promoted by Fusobacterium nucleatum in cancer progression.

A malignant oral epithelial tumor type mentioned as a site where biofilms are enriched with anaerobic periodontal pathogens. It serves as the disease context in which Fusobacterium nucleatum is observed and hypothesized to contribute to cancer development.

Structured microbial communities present on oral squamous cell carcinomas. They are described as enriched with anaerobic periodontal pathogens, including Fusobacterium nucleatum, and are relevant to the tumor-associated microbial environment.

An example of pathogen-driven inflammatory signaling cited to illustrate the broader concept that inflammation can initiate and promote malignancy. It is used as a comparative precedent for Fusobacterium nucleatum-mediated inflammation.

A malignancy cited as an example of cancer associated with Helicobacter pylori-mediated inflammation. It serves as a comparative disease endpoint in the discussion of inflammation-driven carcinogenesis.

A malignancy cited as an example of cancer associated with Fusobacterium nucleatum-mediated inflammation. It provides a comparative context for the bacterium's pro-carcinogenic role beyond the oral cavity.

The anatomical and microbial setting from which Fusobacterium nucleatum was first isolated. It is the local environment relevant to periodontal colonization and oral cancer-associated microbial interactions.

A microbial pathogenic role assigned to Fusobacterium nucleatum in the oral/periodontal environment. This designation is relevant because periodontal pathogens are enriched in oral tumor biofilms and may contribute to carcinogenesis.

A bacterial community-development process involving initiation, maturation, and termination stages, with regulated matrix production and spatial organization. In the text, it is the central biological process being discussed and is influenced by environmental cues, adaptive responses, and group-level activities.

The early phase of biofilm development in which bacteria begin transitioning into a biofilm state. It is described as being triggered by environmental cues and linked to induction of biofilm matrix production.
The late phase in which biofilm development is brought to an end. It is described as being associated with termination of biofilm matrix production and transition out of the biofilm state.

The synthesis of extracellular matrix material that supports biofilm structure and development. The text indicates that initiation and termination of biofilm formation respectively induce or terminate this process.

A second messenger molecule that mediates regulation of biofilm matrix production. In the abstract, it is the molecular signal through which environmental cues influence biofilm initiation and termination.

Environmental conditions or signals that bacteria respond to during biofilm development. They provide the contextual trigger for initiation and termination processes and shape biofilm formation pathways.

Distinct intermediate phases defined between initiation and termination of biofilm formation. These stages reflect the temporal organization of biofilm development and are influenced by adaptive responses.

Flexible bacterial responses to environmental conditions that govern transitions during biofilm development. The text suggests these responses are the main drivers of stage transitions rather than fixed genetic programs.
Genetically programmed regulatory pathways that are contrasted with adaptive responses in the text. The evidence suggests biofilm stage transitions are not mainly governed by these programs.
Alternative biological routes through which biofilm formation can proceed. The abstract states that biofilm formation can occur through multiple pathways, indicating mechanistic heterogeneity.

The organized physical architecture of biofilms, including spatial arrangement and morphology. It is described as dependent on species and environmental conditions, making it a key phenotypic endpoint of biofilm development.

Contextual conditions in which biofilms develop, including factors that influence structure and developmental pathways. The text identifies them as determinants of biofilm spatial structure and developmental behavior.
A species-specific contextual attribute indicating that biofilm spatial structure varies across bacterial species. It functions as a modifying context rather than a molecular mechanism.

Distinct bacterial groups within a population that participate in biofilm development. The text highlights subpopulation heterogeneity as important for interactions and structural outcomes during biofilm formation.
A bacterial subpopulation characterized by motility. It is mentioned as one of the interacting subgroups that can develop during biofilm formation and influence biofilm structure.
A bacterial subpopulation lacking motility. It is described as interacting with motile subpopulations during biofilm development and contributing to biofilm architecture.
Functional interactions among bacterial subpopulations during biofilm development. These interactions can alter the resulting biofilm structure and reflect group-level coordination.
Structural molecular components secreted into the biofilm matrix. Their regulated synthesis is presented as evidence that biofilm formation is programmed at the molecular level.
Controlled production of extracellular matrix components during biofilm development. It is described as a key mechanism supporting the programmed aspect of biofilm formation.
Collective behaviors of bacterial communities that contribute to biofilm formation. The text notes that these activities are involved alongside individual adaptive responses.

Single bacterial cells acting as the unit of adaptive response during biofilm development. The abstract emphasizes that biofilm formation is mainly governed by adaptive responses of individual bacteria.

Structured microbial communities that form multicellular growth states and serve as the central biological subject of the review. They are the source population from which cells disperse and are relevant to biofilm control and infection persistence.

Individual free-living microbial cells that can transition into a multicellular biofilm state and later re-enter a planktonic lifestyle during dispersion. They represent the cellular form that is released from biofilms.

The final step of the biofilm life cycle in which cells egress from the biofilm and resume a planktonic lifestyle. It is a key process discussed as a mechanism for biofilm control and therapeutic intervention.
The developmental sequence of biofilm formation, maintenance, and dispersal. Dispersion is described as its final step, making this process central to understanding biofilm dynamics.

The free-living growth state of microbial cells outside the biofilm matrix. It is the state that dispersed cells resume and is associated with greater vulnerability to antimicrobial agents and immune responses.
Therapeutic agents that inhibit or kill microbes. In the text, the planktonic state is described as more vulnerable to these agents, supporting dispersion as a biofilm-control strategy.
Host defense processes that can act against microbial cells. The planktonic state is noted to be more vulnerable to these responses, linking dispersion to increased susceptibility during infection.
The desired reduction or management of biofilm burden. Dispersion is presented as a promising avenue toward this outcome by releasing cells into a more vulnerable state.
Endogenous signals or conditions that contribute to triggering dispersion. They are discussed as one class of mechanisms influencing the transition out of biofilms.
External signals or conditions that contribute to triggering dispersion. They are discussed alongside native cues as factors that regulate the dispersion process.
Breakdown of the biofilm extracellular matrix, which facilitates cell release during dispersion. The review highlights it as an important mechanism in the dispersion process.

Cells that have exited the biofilm during dispersion and exhibit a distinct phenotype. They are the cellular products of the dispersion process and are relevant to infection and therapeutic susceptibility.
A phenotypic state characteristic of dispersed cells that differs from cells in the biofilm or planktonic states. It is discussed as a notable biological outcome of dispersion.
The host-associated context in which dispersing bacteria may be therapeutically targeted. It provides the clinical or biological environment for the translational relevance of biofilm dispersion.
The potential for applying biofilm dispersion knowledge to practical treatment strategies. It reflects the broader clinical significance of dispersing bacteria during infection.

Structured microbial communities attached to submerged surfaces in the marine environment. In this text, biofilms are the central biological context influencing settlement, colonization, and biofouling-related interactions through surface-associated and diffusible signals.

Microbial organisms that form biofilms and contribute to the mixed-community structure discussed in the marine fouling context. They are important as primary biofilm constituents and potential sources of signals affecting settlement.

Photosynthetic organisms frequently associated with bacterial biofilms on submerged marine structures. They are part of the mixed biofilm community and may contribute to the spatial and chemical complexity of the surface environment.

Single-celled eukaryotic organisms mentioned as frequent associates of marine biofilms. They contribute to the mixed-species community that can alter the signals and interpretability of settlement-related observations.
Fungal organisms noted as common members of marine biofilm communities. Their presence contributes to the mixed biofilm composition that may influence colonization and settlement behavior.

Marine surfaces submerged in the environment that serve as substrates for biofilm formation and subsequent colonization by fouling organisms. This is the physical setting where the described interactions occur.

The aquatic environmental setting in which biofilms, fouling organisms, spores, larvae, and associated microbial communities interact. It provides the ecological context for settlement and biofouling processes.
The process by which spores and larvae establish on submerged surfaces, often via a biofilmed surface. It is a key downstream biological process influenced by biofilm properties and signaling.
The attachment and establishment behavior of cells, spores, and larvae on surfaces. In this text, settlement is modulated by biofilm-derived signals and is central to biofouling initiation.
Behavioral response of cells, spores, and larvae during surface settlement. It is influenced by biofilm-associated signals that may either promote or inhibit attachment.
Chemical or molecular cues produced by biofilms that can act locally on surfaces or diffuse through the environment. These signals are implicated in moderating settlement behavior.

Generic cellular entities whose settling behavior is discussed in relation to biofilm-derived signals. They are part of the broader set of organisms whose surface attachment may be moderated by biofilms.

Dispersal-stage biological units that colonize submerged surfaces and settle via biofilmed surfaces. They are a major target of biofilm-mediated settlement effects and quorum sensing-related stimulation.
Developmental stages of fouling organisms that settle and colonize submerged surfaces. Their settlement is influenced by biofilm properties and microbial signaling.
Organisms that contribute to biofouling by colonizing submerged structures. They include cells, spores, and larvae whose settlement is affected by biofilms.
Biofilms composed of multiple microbial members, especially in field settings. Their mixed composition and spatial organization complicate interpretation of settlement-related studies.
Experimental studies conducted in natural marine conditions. They are noted as difficult to interpret when examining mixed biofilms because of conflicting signals and spatial organization.
The collective microbial community within a biofilm, including different members that produce potentially conflicting signals. It is relevant to the complexity of settlement modulation.
The spatial arrangement of members within the biofilm community. This organization affects the interpretation of biofilm-mediated signals and settlement outcomes.
Laboratory methods used to isolate and identify biofilm bacteria. The text notes their limitations in capturing the full diversity of biofilm-associated organisms.
Methods used to identify biofilm bacteria and reveal limitations of culture-based approaches. They are important for improving detection of organisms involved in settlement effects.
Specific microbial isolates within biofilms that may have the greatest impact on settlement of spores and larvae. The text suggests some impactful strains may not yet have been isolated and cultured.
Compounds isolated from cultured organisms that may not accurately represent natural biofilm conditions. They are discussed as potentially misleading proxies for in situ biofilm chemistry.
Bacterial signaling molecules involved in quorum sensing that are reported to stimulate settlement of spores. They represent a key molecular cue linking biofilm bacteria to settlement behavior.
Green macroalga whose spores are discussed as responding to bacterial quorum sensing signal molecules. It serves as a biological example of settlement stimulation by biofilm-derived cues.
Emerging methods intended to improve understanding of interactions between fouling organisms and biofilms. They are positioned as enabling better analysis of complex marine biofilm systems.
Unwanted accumulation of organisms on submerged structures, representing the applied outcome of interest in this text. The study aims to inform strategies to control this endpoint.
Novel strategies intended to reduce or prevent biofouling. The text frames improved understanding of biofilm-fouling interactions as informing this intervention goal.

The bacterial model organism and pathogen studied in the paper. It serves as the biological system in which quorum sensing and c-di-GMP signaling are examined for their roles in biofilm morphogenesis and clinically relevant pathogenic behavior.

The developmental process by which Vibrio cholerae transitions into structured biofilm communities. It is the central biological process regulated by quorum sensing and c-di-GMP signaling in the study.

A cell-density-dependent communication process that coordinates group behaviors in bacteria. In this study, it acts as a sensory input that modulates biofilm formation and regulates c-di-GMP-metabolizing receptor expression.

A second messenger signaling pathway used by bacteria to detect and respond to environmental stimuli. It is a major regulatory process controlling biofilm development and matrix gene expression in Vibrio cholerae.

An autoinducer molecule used experimentally to modulate quorum sensing. In the study, it represses biofilm formation when acting alone but contributes to synergistic biofilm enhancement when combined with norspermidine.
A polyamine signal used to modulate NspS-MbaA-mediated c-di-GMP production. It induces biofilm formation on its own and synergizes with AI-2 to increase biofilm biomass and cell density.
The receptor-mediated process controlling synthesis of c-di-GMP through the NspS and MbaA system. It links detection of norspermidine to downstream biofilm regulatory responses.
A quantitative endpoint reflecting the total amount of biofilm formed. The study reports that simultaneous detection of AI-2 and norspermidine increases this endpoint.
A biofilm-associated endpoint describing the density of cells within the biofilm structure. It is increased synergistically by combined AI-2 and norspermidine signaling.
The expression of the nspS-mbaA gene system, which is activated by quorum sensing in the described mechanism. Increased expression raises NspS and MbaA levels and promotes c-di-GMP biosynthesis.
A receptor component whose levels increase following quorum-sensing-mediated activation of nspS-mbaA expression. It participates in the regulation of c-di-GMP production in response to norspermidine.
A receptor/enzyme component whose levels increase following quorum-sensing-mediated activation of nspS-mbaA expression. It contributes to c-di-GMP biosynthesis and downstream biofilm regulation.
The synthesis of the second messenger c-di-GMP. In the paper, increased MbaA-synthesized c-di-GMP biosynthesis is a key mechanistic step leading to activation of biofilm regulatory transcription.
A transcription factor activated by increased c-di-GMP levels. It drives elevated expression of genes encoding key biofilm matrix components.

entity_name: GENES ENCODING KEY BIOFILM MATRIX COMPONENTS
description: Gene set encoding structural components of the biofilm matrix. Their expression is elevated downstream of VpsR activation and supports biofilm morphogenesis.
The formation and maturation of biofilm communities. The paper uses this as a functional outcome of combined quorum-sensing and c-di-GMP signaling.
The density of bacterial cells in the population, which is sensed through quorum sensing. It provides contextual information that connects communal state to environmental stimulus detection.

External cues detected by bacterial signaling systems, including norspermidine-related sensing in this study. They are integrated with population-density information to regulate biofilm morphogenesis.

The process by which bacteria develop structured biofilms; in this text it is the central biological process being regulated by quorum sensing, c-di-GMP, sRNAs, and potentially ribonucleases. It is described as a tightly controlled, multi-stage process that confers ecological advantage and contributes to persistence in hostile environments.

Community-based bacterial growth state characterized by a self-produced polymeric matrix and enhanced tolerance to environmental stressors. In the abstract, biofilms are presented as the common life-cycle stage that underlies protective behavior and antimicrobial resistance concerns.

A bacterial cell-density-dependent signaling/regulatory process that controls gene expression and contributes to biofilm formation. In this review, it is one of the four major biofilm regulators and is noted to have overlapping pathways with c-di-GMP and sRNAs.

A bacterial second messenger molecule that functions as a key regulator of biofilm formation. The text identifies it as one of the fundamental regulators across all stages of biofilm development and as part of overlapping regulatory pathways.

Small regulatory RNA molecules involved in bacterial gene regulation. Here they are described as fundamental regulators of biofilm formation, with roles spanning all stages and pathway overlap with quorum sensing and c-di-GMP.

RNA-degrading enzymes discussed as potential biofilm regulators. The abstract highlights them as an emerging focus of interest and notes that their relationships with quorum sensing, c-di-GMP, and sRNAs have been investigated.

The extracellular matrix produced by biofilm-forming bacteria that encases the biofilm structure. It contains polysaccharides, proteins, signalling molecules, extracellular DNA, and extracellular RNA, and is central to biofilm architecture and protection.
Matrix components within bacterial biofilms that contribute to the structural and protective properties of the biofilm extracellular matrix.
Macromolecular components of the biofilm matrix that contribute to biofilm structure and function.
Chemical mediators present in the biofilm matrix that support communication and regulation within biofilms.
DNA present outside bacterial cells as a component of the biofilm matrix, contributing to biofilm stability and architecture.
RNA present outside bacterial cells as a component of the biofilm matrix, contributing to matrix composition and potentially regulatory interactions.

Adverse environmental conditions such as pH and temperature that biofilms help bacteria withstand. In this context, they define the selective environment in which biofilm formation provides an ecological advantage.
Clinical/healthcare environment where biofilm formation on equipment is especially problematic and can contribute to antimicrobial-resistant strains.
Clinical equipment surfaces in hospitals or patient care settings on which biofilms can form and serve as reservoirs for antimicrobial-resistant strains.
A type of patient or hospital equipment mentioned as a surface where biofilms can form, contributing to infection-control challenges.
Clinical devices mentioned as surfaces susceptible to biofilm formation, with relevance to healthcare-associated contamination and resistance.
Bacterial strains with resistance to antimicrobial agents; in the abstract, biofilm formation on clinical equipment can become a source of these strains, making them an important adverse outcome.

The bacterial population discussed as the disease-causing subject group in the article. These organisms are the biological targets of biofilm formation, antibiotic treatment, and antibiofilm strategies, and they are described as adopting biofilms to survive hostile conditions.

A multicellular bacterial lifestyle and structured community state that promotes stress tolerance, antibacterial evasion, and persistence. In the text, biofilm formation and mature biofilm disintegration are central biological processes underlying treatment resistance and therapeutic targeting.
Adverse environmental conditions that biofilms help bacteria tolerate. It functions as a selective pressure that biofilm formation mitigates, contributing to bacterial persistence and survival.
Agents used to kill or inhibit bacteria. The text states that biofilms enable bacteria to evade these agents, reducing their effectiveness against biofilm-associated cells.

A class of antimicrobial drugs used to treat infectious diseases. The article notes that biofilm-mediated defense has rendered antibiotics ineffective in some contexts, highlighting their reduced activity against biofilm-embedded bacteria.

Microbial populations characterized by strong resistance to drug treatment. They are described as emerging rapidly in association with treatment practices and are relevant to the broader infectious disease problem discussed in the review.

A bacterial second messenger and global signaling molecule that regulates biofilm-related gene expression. It is implicated in adhesion, extracellular matrix production, transition to biofilm stage, stability, pathogenicity, virulence, and nutrient acquisition.
Regulatory RNA molecules involved in controlling bacterial biofilm formation. They are listed among the signaling mechanisms that modulate biofilm development.

A cell density-dependent bacterial communication process that regulates biofilm formation and associated gene expression. It is linked to c-di-GMP signaling and influences multiple biofilm-associated phenotypes.
A contextual biological property describing quorum sensing as dependent on bacterial population density. It captures the operational condition under which QS signaling becomes relevant.

The transcriptional output regulated by biofilm-associated signaling pathways such as c-di-GMP and quorum sensing. It underlies changes in adhesion, matrix production, pathogenicity, virulence, and nutrient acquisition.
The process by which bacteria attach to surfaces or each other during biofilm initiation. It is regulated by c-di-GMP-associated signaling and contributes to biofilm establishment.
The synthesis of matrix material that structurally supports biofilms. It is a key biofilm-associated process regulated by signaling pathways described in the article.

entity_name: TRANSITION FROM THE PLANKTONIC TO BIOFILM STAGE
description: The shift from free-living bacterial growth to the biofilm lifestyle. This transition is regulated by c-di-GMP and quorum sensing and is central to biofilm development.
The maintenance and persistence of the biofilm structure. In the text, biofilm stability is one of the regulated outcomes of c-di-GMP-linked signaling.
The disease-causing potential of bacteria. The article identifies pathogenicity as a biofilm-associated outcome influenced by signaling pathways such as c-di-GMP and quorum sensing.
The degree of harmfulness or disease severity caused by bacteria. It is described as being regulated in association with biofilm formation and related signaling mechanisms.
The process by which bacteria obtain nutrients, which is influenced by biofilm-associated signaling and gene regulation. It contributes to bacterial survival within biofilms.
A therapeutic strategy aimed at preventing the development of bacterial biofilms. The article presents it as a key antibiofilm approach that improves antimicrobial access to bacteria.
A therapeutic strategy intended to break down established biofilms. It is discussed as a means to expose bacteria to antimicrobials at lower effective concentrations.
Agents used to inhibit or kill microorganisms. In the article, their effectiveness improves when biofilms are inhibited or disrupted, allowing access to free-living bacterial cells.
Bacterial cells not protected by the biofilm matrix and therefore more accessible to antimicrobial treatment. They represent the vulnerable target state after biofilm disruption.

Bacteria residing within biofilms and protected by the biofilm structure. They require higher antimicrobial concentrations than free-living cells and are central to the treatment-resistance problem described.

The disease category discussed as being caused by bacteria and complicated by biofilm-mediated resistance. The review frames antibiofilm and antimicrobial strategies as approaches to managing these diseases.

The broader health context impacted by biofilm-related bacterial infections and their treatment. The article notes that the molecules and strategies discussed have broad implications for human health.

The bacterial organisms discussed as the infectious population capable of forming biofilms and causing disease. They are the biological subjects whose biofilm behavior, motility, and antimicrobial tolerance are central to the review.

Bacterial cells residing within biofilms, characterized by aggregation and enclosure in a protective matrix. They are the functional cellular population affected by dispersal, disruption, and antimicrobial treatment.

A multicellular bacterial growth state involving aggregation and formation of a protective exopolymeric matrix. Biofilm formation is a central biological process in the text because it promotes persistence, antimicrobial tolerance, and infection chronicity.

The process by which bacteria transition into a biofilm lifestyle, including surface attachment, matrix production, and reduced motility. It is mediated by c-di-GMP signaling and contributes to antimicrobial tolerance.
The process in which cells leave the biofilm state and migrate to new sites. In the text, it is associated with c-di-GMP degradation, increased motility, and matrix breakdown.
The direct breakdown of the biofilm matrix that forcibly releases embedded cells. It is presented as an anti-biofilm strategy that exposes bacteria to antimicrobials.
The reduced susceptibility of biofilm-associated bacteria to antimicrobial treatment. It is a clinically important endpoint that makes conventional therapy less effective.
Infectious disease outcomes caused by bacteria, associated here with high morbidity and mortality globally. The review frames biofilms as a major contributor to persistent bacterial infection.
Infections in which bacteria persist in biofilm form, leading to treatment resistance and eradication challenges. This is the disease-relevant endpoint targeted by anti-biofilm strategies.
The adverse population-level health burden associated with bacterial infections. It is mentioned as the global consequence motivating improved treatment strategies.
A ubiquitous bacterial secondary messenger signaling system that regulates biofilm formation and dispersal. It is a key molecular control point linking intracellular signaling to biofilm phenotypes.

Cyclic di-GMP, the bacterial secondary messenger whose synthesis and degradation regulate biofilm-associated behaviors. It functions as the central molecular regulator in the described biofilm transitions.
Enzymes that synthesize c-di-GMP in bacteria. Their activity promotes biofilm formation by increasing c-di-GMP levels.
Enzymes that degrade c-di-GMP in bacteria. Their activity lowers c-di-GMP levels and promotes biofilm dispersal.
Bacterial movement behavior that is inversely associated with biofilm formation and enhanced during dispersal. It is a functional process used to leave biofilms and colonize new sites.
The process by which bacteria adhere to surfaces, contributing to biofilm establishment. Increased surface attachment is described as part of c-di-GMP-driven biofilm formation.
The self-secreted exopolymeric matrix that encases biofilm cells and protects them from antibiotics. It is a structural molecular feature central to biofilm integrity and resistance.
The breakdown of the biofilm matrix, either during dispersal or disruption. This process releases embedded cells and undermines biofilm protection.
The attached, non-motile lifestyle of bacteria within biofilms. It is contrasted with motile dispersal behavior and is reversed during active dispersal.
Conventional antibacterial agents used to treat infections. In the text, their penetration is impeded by biofilm matrix, and their effectiveness improves after biofilm disruption or dispersal.
Broad antimicrobial agents used in clinical settings to eradicate bacterial cells. They are more effective once biofilm protection is removed.
Therapeutic agents intended to counter biofilm formation, persistence, or tolerance. They are proposed as needed interventions against biofilm infections.

An anti-biofilm strategy that signals bacterial cells to leave the biofilm, promoting motility and self-degradation of the matrix. It is intended to weaken biofilms and improve antimicrobial susceptibility.
An anti-biofilm strategy that directly degrades the biofilm matrix and forcibly releases embedded cells. It is used to dismantle biofilm structure and expose bacteria to treatment.
The healthcare context in which anti-biofilm strategies are intended to be applied alongside antimicrobials. It represents the translational environment for managing biofilm infections.

An opportunistic human bacterial pathogen that serves as the organismal subject of the review. It is the population in which c-di-GMP signaling, biofilm formation, and related regulatory mechanisms are discussed.
Hospital-acquired infections caused primarily by Pseudomonas aeruginosa in this context. It represents the clinically relevant disease outcome associated with the pathogen.

A multicellular growth and attachment process in which Pseudomonas aeruginosa transitions to a sessile community state. It is central to chronic, difficult-to-eradicate infection and is regulated by c-di-GMP signaling.

entity_name: CHRONIC AND HARD TO ERADICATE INFECTIONS
description: Persistent infection phenotype associated with biofilm formation by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It captures the clinical consequence of biofilm-mediated resistance to clearance.

An intracellular bacterial secondary messenger that regulates the motile-to-sessile transition and biofilm-associated behaviors. Its dynamic cellular concentration is the key molecular signal discussed in the review.
The signaling role of c-di-GMP as an intracellular regulatory molecule in bacterial cells. It functions as a molecular mediator linking environmental or enzymatic inputs to cellular responses.
A bacterial phenotypic switch from motile behavior to surface-associated sessile growth. In this text, it is a key process controlled by c-di-GMP signaling and linked to biofilm development.

A class of enzymes that synthesize c-di-GMP and thereby increase its intracellular levels. They are antagonistic to phosphodiesterases and are important regulators of biofilm initiation, maturation, and dispersion.
A class of enzymes that degrade c-di-GMP and reduce its cellular concentration. They act antagonistically to diguanylate cyclases and help control biofilm-associated signaling dynamics.
The intracellular abundance of c-di-GMP, which is dynamically regulated by DGCs and PDEs. These levels determine downstream signaling outputs and biofilm-related cellular states.
The early stage of biofilm development in which cells begin surface-associated community formation. It is one of the stages regulated by c-di-GMP levels and associated enzymes.
The developmental stage in which biofilms become structurally established and functionally mature. It is regulated by c-di-GMP signaling and associated enzymatic control.
The stage in which cells leave the biofilm community and disperse. It is controlled by c-di-GMP signaling dynamics and contributes to biofilm lifecycle regulation.
Proteins that sense perturbations in c-di-GMP levels and convert the signal into functional cellular outputs. They mediate downstream responses to changes in the second messenger.
Changes or fluctuations in intracellular c-di-GMP concentration that are detected by effector proteins. These perturbations drive downstream signaling responses.
The downstream cellular response elicited after effector proteins sense c-di-GMP perturbations. It represents the biological consequence of signaling pathway activation.
The specific cellular response matched to dynamic c-di-GMP signaling changes. It reflects the pathway's ability to regulate bacterial behavior in a context-dependent manner.
Therapeutic or preventive strategies aimed at disrupting biofilm formation or maintenance. The review identifies c-di-GMP signaling components as potential targets for these interventions.
Previously uncharacterized molecular targets implicated in c-di-GMP signaling and biofilm regulation. They are proposed as candidates for anti-biofilm intervention development.

A bacterial species used here as the representative model organism for biofilm study and the biological subject in which biofilm dispersion phenomena are discussed. It serves as the experimental/observational population for understanding dispersal mechanisms and environmental responses.

A sessile microbial community state characterized by attached growth on surfaces and embedded extracellular matrix. In this text it is the central biological process whose formation, maintenance, and dispersion are being reviewed.

An active detachment process in which cells separate from the biofilm and return to planktonic life. It is described as a complex, regulated biological process involving spatial differentiation, molecular events, and environmental cues.
The broader process of cells leaving the biofilm structure. In this abstract it is used as the general category that includes dispersal and distinguishes active from passive detachment modes.
The free-living bacterial state that cells return to after dispersal from the biofilm. It represents the downstream physiological state resulting from active detachment.
The self-produced structural matrix surrounding biofilm cells. It is a localized molecular feature that cements cells together and contributes to biofilm stability and resistance to detachment.

The major molecular components of the biofilm extracellular matrix. EPSs include polysaccharides, extracellular DNA, and proteins, and they are functionally important for biofilm cohesion and dispersal resistance.
A class of extracellular polymeric substances contributing to the biofilm matrix. They are part of the structural scaffold that supports biofilm integrity.
Extracellular DNA present within the biofilm matrix. It is a molecular component of EPSs and contributes to matrix structure and biofilm stability.
Protein components of the extracellular polymeric substance matrix. They are part of the biofilm scaffold and may participate in structural and regulatory functions.

A developmental/organizational process within biofilm cells that creates spatially distinct states. In the abstract it is described as a prerequisite for dispersal and a key mechanism underlying active detachment.
The set of molecular-level changes associated with biofilm dispersal. This broad process category captures the signaling and regulatory events that enable active detachment in response to cues.
External environmental conditions or signals that trigger or regulate biofilm dispersal. They provide the contextual input that induces molecular and spatial changes in biofilm cells.
A passive mode of biofilm detachment mentioned as distinct from active dispersal. It represents a non-regulated loss of biomass from the biofilm.
Another passive biofilm detachment mode contrasted with active dispersal. It refers to bulk removal of biofilm material rather than regulated cell separation.
The research context in which Pseudomonas aeruginosa is used as a model organism. It frames the observational and mechanistic investigation of biofilm formation and dispersal.
The pathogenic role attributed to Pseudomonas aeruginosa in humans. This descriptor highlights its clinical relevance and why it is important in biofilm-related research.
A cyclic dinucleotide secondary messenger that regulates bacterial lifestyle transitions, especially the switch between sessile and motile states, and is central to biofilm-associated signaling.
A bacterial behavioral transition between surface-attached sessile growth and free-swimming motile growth, regulated by c-di-GMP and linked to biofilm formation and multicellular behavior.
The process by which bacteria assemble structured multicellular communities; in this text it is a major physiological output of c-di-GMP signaling and regulatory control.
Collective bacterial behaviors beyond single-cell growth, described here as being influenced by c-di-GMP signaling and biofilm-associated regulation.
A signaling molecule class to which c-di-GMP belongs; it functions in intracellular regulation and signaling specificity in bacterial systems.
A group of bacterial proteins that synthesize or degrade c-di-GMP, thereby controlling its intracellular levels and downstream signaling output.
Regulatory factors that coordinate expression of c-di-GMP metabolizing proteins and integrate broader control of bacterial signaling and behavior.

entity_name: SELECTED PANELS OF C-DI-GMP METABOLIZING PROTEINS
description: Specific subsets of c-di-GMP metabolizing proteins whose expression is concertedly modified by global regulators to tune signaling specificity.
Downstream molecular targets acted on by c-di-GMP metabolizing proteins, representing functional effectors in bacterial physiology.
Bacterial movement-related process that is directly regulated by global regulators and functionally linked to c-di-GMP signaling and biofilm control.
Post-translational regulatory mechanism affecting c-di-GMP metabolizing proteins and contributing to control of signaling specificity and protein function.
A post-translational modification mechanism that regulates c-di-GMP metabolizing proteins and influences their activity or stability.
Spatial regulation of c-di-GMP metabolizing proteins within the cell, described as a post-translational control mechanism affecting signaling output.
The persistence or turnover of c-di-GMP metabolizing proteins, controlled post-translationally and relevant to signaling regulation.
The overall phenotypic output of bacterial regulatory networks, including motility and biofilm-related states, determined by c-di-GMP signaling.
The multicellular bacterial community context in which phenotypic diversity and c-di-GMP signaling specificity are discussed at the single-cell level.

Structured microbial communities embedded in a matrix that drive chronic infection persistence, increase tolerance to antibiotics compared with planktonic cells, and are the central biological target discussed in the review.

Long-lasting infectious disease states associated with host tissue, fluids, or indwelling medical devices; these infections are described as being strongly linked to biofilm formation and difficult to treat.
Biological host environments in which biofilm-associated chronic infections occur and persist, providing a context for microbial colonization and therapeutic targeting.
Clinical device-associated environment that supports biofilm formation and contributes to chronic infection persistence and treatment difficulty.
Antimicrobial agents whose effectiveness is reduced against biofilms relative to planktonic cells, highlighting the therapeutic challenge addressed by the review.
Microbial cells existing in a free-living, non-biofilm state used as the comparison population for biofilm-associated antibiotic tolerance.
Nucleic acid-based binding molecules with high affinity, selectivity, and stability that are proposed as antibiofilm therapeutics and targeting tools for drug delivery systems.
Therapeutic agents intended to inhibit, disrupt, or eradicate biofilms; aptamers are discussed as candidates in this role.
Therapeutic platforms or delivery constructs that can be targeted by aptamers to improve specificity and biofilm-directed treatment.
Microbial movement-related process that can be inhibited by aptamer-based strategies to interfere with biofilm development or maintenance.
Attachment process by which microbes adhere to surfaces or host substrates; inhibition of adhesion is described as a mechanism of aptamer action against biofilms.
Signaling molecules involved in microbial quorum sensing that regulate coordinated biofilm behaviors and can be blocked by aptamer-based approaches.
Cell-density-dependent microbial communication process that regulates biofilm behavior and is targeted indirectly through blocking of quorum sensing molecules.
Cells residing within the biofilm state that can be dispersed back to a planktonic state as part of antibiofilm intervention.
Free-living microbial state resulting from dispersal of biofilm cells; represents a less protected phenotype relative to biofilm-associated growth.
Overall therapeutic control or eradication of biofilms in clinical or applied settings; the review discusses limitations, challenges, and opportunities affecting this outcome.
Chemical or structural modifications to aptamers intended to improve their applicability, success, and performance in biofilm-related applications.

A non-flagellated bacterial species used as the biological subject in this study. It is the organism in which PilB, cyclic-di-GMP signaling, motility, piliation, and biofilm formation are investigated.

The type IV pilus (T4P) assembly ATPase in Myxococcus xanthus. It functions as a cdG effector candidate, contains a conserved MshEN cdG-binding domain in its N-terminus, and is central to regulating T4P-dependent motility and biofilm formation.

Cyclic-di-GMP, a bacterial second messenger that plays a crucial regulatory role in switching between motile and biofilm lifestyles. In this study it is proposed to directly interact with PilB and modulate downstream phenotypes.
A newly discovered c-di-GMP-binding domain conserved in the N-terminus of PilB. It is the structural feature implicated in c-di-GMP recognition and in controlling PilB-dependent outputs.
A bacterial motility apparatus that enables surface movement in Myxococcus xanthus. It is also implicated in exopolysaccharide regulation and biofilm-related functions.
Motility powered by the type IV pilus machinery on solid surfaces. It is a key biological output regulated by PilB and influenced by c-di-GMP signaling.
The developmental process leading to biofilm production and maintenance in Myxococcus xanthus. It is one of the principal outputs modulated by PilB and c-di-GMP.
The broader developmental process underlying biofilm establishment and maturation. It is described as being regulated by c-di-GMP and PilB-mediated signaling.
The process or state of pilus production/assembly in Myxococcus xanthus. It is used as a phenotype in the mutational analysis of PilB and reflects T4P-related function.
The biofilm matrix material regulated in part by type IV pilus-associated mechanisms in this bacterium. It contributes to biofilm structure and is linked to PilB/T4P-associated regulation.

The N-terminal region of PilB containing the conserved MshEN c-di-GMP-binding domain. It is the domain subjected to systematic mutational analysis and is implicated in dual regulation of motility and biofilm levels.

Engineered amino-acid substitution mutations introduced into the PilBN domain to test the functional role of c-di-GMP binding. These mutations alter PilB-associated phenotypes, especially piliation and biofilm levels.
A mutant phenotype characterized by reduced PilB protein abundance. The study excludes these mutants from certain phenotype interpretations because low protein levels confound functional assessment.

entity_name: DISTINCT AND DIFFERENTIAL PHENOTYPES IN PILIATION AND BIOFILM LEVELS
description: Observed mutant phenotypes showing variable effects on pilus formation and biofilm abundance. These outcomes are used to infer functional separation and dependence among PilB-mediated processes.
The general movement behavior of Myxococcus xanthus on solid surfaces. It is regulated by PilB and c-di-GMP and is functionally linked to T4P-dependent motility.

The microbial subject population discussed in the review. Bacteria are the organisms in which quorum sensing, cyclic-di-GMP, and nitric oxide signaling are examined as regulators of biofilm production, motility, colonization, defense, and environmental adaptation.

The developmental process by which bacteria produce structured biofilms. In this text it is a central biological outcome controlled by quorum sensing, cyclic-di-GMP, and nitric oxide signaling, and it is linked to bacterial adaptation and host colonization.

The process of generating bacterial biofilms, emphasized as the main functional output of the signaling network reviewed in the abstract. It reflects coordinated regulation of extracellular matrix formation and community behavior.

A bacterial cell-density sensing and signaling process used to detect population changes. It is described as a regulatory pathway that contributes to biofilm formation and broader bacterial functions such as motility and adaptation.

A bacterial second messenger and signaling molecule mentioned as one of the key signals involved in regulating biofilm formation. It functions within the signaling network that coordinates developmental and adaptive bacterial responses.

A signaling molecule referenced as part of the regulatory network influencing bacterial behavior. In this context it participates in signaling pathways associated with biofilm formation and environmental response.
The broader regulatory signaling mechanisms discussed in the review. These pathways integrate quorum sensing, cyclic-di-GMP, and nitric oxide signals to control biofilm formation and motility.
A bacterial behavioral process controlled by the signaling pathways discussed in the abstract. It is presented as one of the functions regulated alongside biofilm formation.

A biologically relevant outcome for bacteria, described as a benefit associated with the regulated features of biofilm formation and motility. It reflects successful establishment on or within a host.
An adaptive outcome describing bacterial competitive advantage. The abstract links this benefit to signaling-controlled biofilm formation and related functions.

A bacterial adaptive outcome enabled by the signaling network described in the review. It captures the functional significance of quorum sensing, cyclic-di-GMP, and nitric oxide in environmental responsiveness.

The external conditions sensed by bacteria that influence signaling behavior. The abstract notes that bacteria use quorum sensing and related signals to respond to particular environmental conditions.
The bacterial community-level state detected by quorum sensing. It serves as a contextual population attribute that triggers signaling responses relevant to biofilm formation.

The complex matrix surrounding bacterial biofilms that contributes to biofilm flexibility and environmental adaptation. It is described as a structural feature that can be tailored to changing demands.
